title: A Radio Interview About Screen Time and Sleep
script: Radio Host: [cheerfully] Good evening, listeners. Tonight we're joined by Dr. Lestari, a sleep specialist, to talk about screens and sleep. Welcome!
Dr. Lestari: [warmly] Thank you for inviting me. This topic affects almost everyone who owns a phone these days.
Radio Host: [curious] Let's start simply. Why exactly does looking at a screen before bed affect our sleep so much?
Dr. Lestari: [informative] Screens emit blue light, which tricks the brain into thinking it's still daytime, delaying the release of sleep hormones.
Radio Host: [surprised] So our brain literally believes the sun is still up, even at midnight?
Dr. Lestari: [nodding] Essentially, yes. That confusion makes falling asleep harder, even when our body feels physically exhausted.
Radio Host: [interested] Does it matter what we're actually doing on the screen, or is the light itself the whole problem?
Dr. Lestari: [thoughtful] Both matter. Scrolling through stressful news or arguments online also keeps the mind alert, when it should be calming down.
Radio Host: [curious] What would you recommend to someone who scrolls in bed every single night out of habit?
Dr. Lestari: [gently] Start by charging your phone outside the bedroom, so picking it up simply isn't convenient anymore.
Radio Host: [laughing] That sounds simple, although I imagine it's harder in practice than it sounds.
Dr. Lestari: [understanding] It is, at first. Most patients tell me the first week feels strange, almost like losing a habit they didn't know they had.
Radio Host: [curious] What can someone do instead, during those quiet minutes before sleeping?
Dr. Lestari: [warmly] Reading a physical book works well, or simply lying quietly and reflecting on the day without any screen nearby.
Radio Host: [interested] Does the amount of sleep we lose really matter that much, if we still function during the day?
Dr. Lestari: [serious] Absolutely, because poor sleep affects memory, mood, and even how our body manages hunger and stress over time.
Radio Host: [curious] Is there an ideal time to stop using screens before bed?
Dr. Lestari: [informative] Ideally, one hour before sleeping, although even thirty minutes without a screen makes a noticeable difference for most people.
Radio Host: [smiling] That's very practical advice. Any final thought for our listeners tonight?
Dr. Lestari: [warmly] Sleep isn't a luxury, it's basic maintenance for your whole body, so protecting it deserves real effort, not guilt.
